The pooled quality control (QC) was generated by combining 30 µL aliquots from every sample in the data set into one pooled sample. Samples and system blanks were each injected at 4 µL; the QC pool was injected 9 times at different volumes (3 injections each at 2 µL, 4 µL, and 6 µL). MS data were collected with an anticipated LC peak width of 8 s and a default charge of 1. MS data were acquired at 120,000 resolution from m/z 100-1000 with an RF lens of 60% and maximum injection time of 50 ms.
Data Acquisition: Liquid chromatography – tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS)
Prior to acquiring LC-MS data for samples, liquid chromatography – tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) data were acquired using the AcquireX (Thermo Scientific) deep scan methodology. The acquisition order for AcquireX was the following: system blank (n=1 injection) for exclusion list generation, QC (n=1 injection) for inclusion list generation, and n=7 injections of QC. IMS and MS/MS data were collected with an anticipated LC peak width of 8 s and a default charge of 1. MS data were acquired at 120,000 resolution from m/z 100-1000 with an RF lens of 60% and maximum injection time of 50 ms. MS/MS data were acquired at 30,000 resolution using an isolation width of 1.5 (m/z), stepped assisted higher-energy collision induced dissociation was used with energy steps of 20, 35, and 60 normalized collision energy, and a maximum injection time of 54 ms. The inclusion list was generated and updated via AcquireX with a low and high mass tolerance of 5 part-per-million (ppm) mass error. An intensity filter was applied with an intensity threshold of 2.0 x 104. Dynamic exclusion was used with the following parameters: exclude after n = 3 times; if occurs within 15 s; exclusion duration of 6 s; a low mass tolerance of 5 ppm mass error; a high mass tolerance of 5 ppm mass error; and excluding isotopes.
Data Processing
Processing of Raw Data – Feature Finding
Data files (.raw) were processed with Compound Discoverer 3.3.0.550 (ThermoFisher Scientific) to identify unique molecular features and, where possible, annotate them with chemical names. Features with distinct measured accurate mass, unique retention time, and MS/MS data were tabulated after removal of isotope peaks, blank contaminants, and noise artifacts from the data (workflow and parameters displayed in Supplementary Data 11). The table contained feature descriptors (e.g. m/z and retention time), annotation information (e.g. MS/MS database match), and peak area. Features were then processed using R via Jupyter Notebook. Processing steps included formatting of the table output from Compound Discoverer, comparison of m/z and retention time of annotated features versus an in-house generated list of m/z and retention time based on authentic chemical standards, assessment of signal response in pooled QC samples, assessment of signal variance in pooled QC samples versus samples (i.e. dispersion ratio), and multi- and univariate statistics.
Data Quality and Data Filtering
Signal Response Evaluation
We evaluated the signal response of the pooled sample with the intention of evaluating the fundamental principle of LC-MS/MS that if more of a given feature is present, a corresponding increase in the signal should be obtained. To do this, the pooled QC sample was injected and analyzed at three volumes in technical triplicate: 2 µL, 4 µL, and 6 µL, where 4 µL is the amount of material injected during the untargeted metabolomics assay in the present experiment. For any given feature, the peak area of the feature (i.e. the integration of a signal of unique m/z over a specific retention time) in the 4 µL sample is assumed to represent the mean value of that feature in the dataset; the peak area of that feature in the 2 µL sample and 6 µL sample should therefore represent 50% and 150% of the mean value, respectively. The metric used to evaluate the signal response was coefficient of determination (R2, evaluates fit to a linear model). For every feature in the dataset, a value of these metrics was calculated to evaluate the signal response for that feature over the QC range. Any feature for which the value does not meet the filtering parameter is filtered out of the dataset, ensuring that only features displaying positive correlations within the R2 = 0.7 parameter are retained for further evaluation and interpretation.
Assessment of Dispersion Ratio
The pooled QC was utilized to calculate the dispersion ratio for the sample set. The dispersion ratio is a metric for describing the measurement precision of a detected metabolite; the metric focuses on statistical dispersion of the pooled QC samples in relation to the dispersion of the biological test samples. If the distribution of both the biological test sample measurements and the QC random error are Gaussian, then the dispersion ratio (D-ratio) equal to 50 is the ratio of the sample standard deviation for the pooled QC samples to the sample standard deviation for the biological test samples. (If the data distribution is not Gaussian, then the raw data must be mathematically transformed.) D-ratio is a measurement of technical variance: a D-ratio of 0% means that the technical variance is zero (a “perfect” measurement), and all observed variances can therefore be attributed to a non-measurement (putatively biological) cause, whereas a D-ratio of 100% indicates that all variances can be attributed to the measurement.
Annotation
Features were annotated based on MS/MS spectral matching, in alignment with the Metabolomics Standards Initiative guidelines (Level 2). Prior to annotation, the data acquisition strategy AcquireX (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used to improve coverage compared to similar data acquisition strategies (i.e. data-dependent acquisition). The public, commercial, and in-house MS/MS spectral libraries NIST2020, GNPS (accessed 04-01-2022), mzCloud (offline, endogenous metabolites) were used to evaluate MS/MS spectral matches, as well as an in-house MS/MS spectral library acquired from authentic chemical standards purchased and analyzed by the MCFS. The MS/MS spectral matching was performed in Compound Discoverer (Thermo RFisher Scientific).
During processing in the Jupyter Notebook, each feature was assigned an MSI level of confidence based on the measured data (without manual review). MSI Level 2 features have an MS/MS match to either a database entry or an in-house library reference match. MSI Level 4 and Level 5 features have either an MS/MS match but no database match, or no MS/MS match. MSI Level 2 features were promoted to MSI Level 1 after matching in-house m/z and retention time lists acquired on the same analytical platform using identical analytical conditions. The MSI Level 1 annotations are referred to as identified.
Abundance matrices of 277 annotated metabolites from positive and negative modes were combined (Supplementary Data 1) and used to generate PCA plot in MetaboAnalyst 6.0 without any filtering or normalization. For heatmap generation, 50 top differential annotated metabolites were used.

Flow cytometry analysis
Blood samples were collected in EDTA coated tubes. Red blood cells were lysed with ACK lysis buffer at room temperature for 10 min. The collected lymphocytes were incubated with anti-mouse CD16/32 at room temperature for 10 min to block the IgG Fc receptors. Expression of surface markers was detected by simultaneously staining with the following antibodies (eFluor 450 anti-mouse CD45, AF 700 anti-mouse CD4, FITC anti-mouse CD3, PE-Cy7 anti-mouse MHCII, BV711 anti-mouse CD8, PerCP-Cy™5.5 anti-mouse CD11b, APC anti-mouse CD19, BV510 anti-mouse CD11c, PE anti-mouse Ly6G, PE-Cyanine5 anti-mouse F4/80, APC/Cyanine7 anti-mouse Ly6C, PE-Dazzle 594 anti-mouse CD115) on ice for 30 min followed by wash and flow cytometry.
For flow cytometry analysis of colonic immune cells, colons were flushed with ice-cold PBS (Mg²⁺/Ca²⁺-free) and surrounding fat and mesentery were removed. Colons were then opened longitudinally and transferred to a 50 mL Falcon tube containing 20 mL ice-cold PBS. The tissue was shaken vigorously five times in fresh PBS until the intestines appeared clean and pale (white/pink). Colons were cut into 0.5–1 cm pieces and incubated in 10 mL of pre-digestion buffer (Mg²⁺/Ca²⁺-free HBSS with 2% FBS, 10 mM HEPES, 2 mM EDTA, and 1 mM DTT) at 37°C in a shaking incubator (250 rpm) for 15 minutes followed by three washes with cold PBS. Tissue was digested in 10 mL RPMI-1640 containing 5% FBS, 10 mM HEPES, 0.6 mg/mL Collagenase IV, 0.4 mg/mL Collagenase I, 1 mg/mL Dispase II, and 50 µg/mL DNase I at 37°C with shaking at 250 rpm for 15 minutes. After vortexing for 10 seconds, cells were filtered through a 70 µm strainer and collected in RPMI-1640 with 10% FBS and 10 mM HEPES on ice. The cell suspension was centrifuged at 500 × g for 5 minutes. Before flow cytometry, cells were diluted to 10⁶ cells per 100 μL and incubated with a blocking cocktail containing anti-mouse CD16/CD32 to prevent non-specific binding. Following blocking, cells were stained for surface markers described above for 10 minutes at room temperature.
Flow cytometric analysis was performed on BD LSRFortessa instrument (BD Biosciences) and analyzed using FACSDiva (BD Biosciences) software. All antibodies are listed in Supplementary Data 12. The FACS gating strategy is shown in Supplementary Fig. 10.

Analysis of publicly available expression and clinical data
To analyze the expression of NAD metabolic enzymes in IBD samples, RNA-seq dataset GSE111889 was utilized 42.
To analyze the expression of NAMPT and NAPRT in different human solid tumors in comparison with their respective normal tissues, TCGA data were downloaded from UCSC Xena web portal. The expression values of NAMPT and NAPRT are HTSeq FPKM-UQ normalized values. Normal tissue samples taken from tissue adjacent the tumor were used as normal tissue controls, and only a limited number of normal samples have been sequenced. Primary tumors matching adjacent normal tissues (some normal tissues might have two or more matched tumor samples) as well as all primary tumor samples with expression values were used in separate analyses. Based on the expression values in normal tissue samples, the expression of NAMPT or NAPRT in tumors were stratified into three categories: Below, in which tumor values were below the 25th percentile of the corresponding normal tissue data; Normal, in which tumor values were within the 25th to 75th percentile of the corresponding normal data; and Above, in which tumor values were above the 75th percentile of the corresponding normal data.
Similar results were obtained in matched primary tumors and all primary tumors (Supplementary Data 6).
To analyze the expression of NAMPT and NAPRT in colonic polyps in comparison with normal colonic tissues, single-cell RNA-seq datasets from Becker et al. 60 and Chen et al. 61 were downloaded from public resources. Chen’s dataset was obtained from the CELLxGENE collection (HTAN VUMC: a48f5033-3438-4550-8574-cdff3263fdfd) and further processed using the Scanpy Python package. Becker’s dataset was downloaded from GEO (GSE201348) and processed using the Seurat R package. For both single-cell datasets, mean-based, sample-level pseudobulk counts were aggregated from the raw cell counts and then normalized to CPM (counts per million). The CPM expression values for the genes of interest were retrieved and compared between polyp and normal samples.
For association of NAPRT expression and cancer patients’ survival, RNAseq expression and clinical data for TCGA PanCancer datasets of colon, liver and kidney cancers were downloaded from https://www.cbioportal.org/ 62, 63. Survival analysis was performed in GraphPad Prism v 9.5.1 using cutoffs of NAPRT expression that resulted in best separation of NAPRT-low and NAPRT-high samples for each dataset.

Statistics and Reproducibility
Values are presented as mean with either standard deviation (SD) or standard error of mean (SEM) from a minimum of three independent experiments or biological replicates, unless specified differently in the figure legend. To evaluate significant differences between the means, two-tailed, unpaired, non-parametric Mann-Whitney test was employed when sample size 4, while two-tailed, unpaired, Student’s t-test was utilized when sample size < 4 64. Statistical significance was set at p<0.05. Differences between the means with more than two comparison groups were analyzed by either Kruskal-Wallis test or two-way ANOVA with correction for multiple comparisons by controlling the false discovery rate and adjusted p-values (q-values) were reported. For all figures, *p (or q)<0.05, **p (or q)<0.01, *** p (or q)<0.001, **** p (or q)<0.0001, n.s., not significant. The exact p values are included in the Source Data file. Data analyses were performed using Prism Software 10.0 (GraphPad) or Microsoft Office Excel (Version 16.79.1). No methods were applied to ascertain whether the data met the assumptions of the statistical approach (e.g., normal distribution test).
For animal studies, the sample size in each independent experiment was determined based on our prior experience and mouse availability. The combined sample size for DSS-colitis study was estimated to achieve 2-fold difference of colitis phenotypes (tissue damage scores or rectal bleeding scores) with 80% of power. The sample size for other phenotypes (metabolic changes or tumor burden) was estimated to achieve 30% difference with 80% of power. For gene expression analysis, the sample size was estimated to achieve 2-fold difference of gene expression level with 80% of power. In vitro cell culture experiments were independently performed at least three times and similar results were observed. Each independent experiment was performed with at least three biological replicates, no explicit calculations were done to determine the sample size.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this paper, Wu X et al. have revealed that Naprt deficiency promotes two major processes in colon tumorigenesis: tumor initiation (DNA damage) and promotion (inflammation). They propose that the increased DNA damage in the Naprt-KO mice is likely due to a reduced PARP activity associated with lower NAD levels in epithelial cells. Given these results, a phenotype that Naprt deficiency leads to an increased incidence of colon tumors is convincing. These are novel and interesting findings. However, there are two major concerns regarding this paper that will require many additional efforts, as outlined below;
The first concern relates to the inverse correlation between Naprt expression and prognosis in several cancers (Fig 6J-L). As noted above, data regarding increased tumor formation in Naprt-KO mice is convincing. However, this does not imply that tumors with Naprt deficiency exhibit higher malignancy or more therapeutic resistance. After diagnosis, the prognosis of cancer patients typically worsens with increasing malignancy and/or treatment resistance of tumor cells. Importantly, tumor cells with DNA repair defects often show higher sensitivity to chemotherapy and radiation therapy, which can extend patient survival. Thus, even if Naprt-low cancers show worse prognoses compared to Naprt-high cancers, it does not seem reasonable to attribute this to an impaired DNA repair ability associated with Naprt deficiency.
Another major issue is that this study overlooks recent important findings on systemic NA metabolism. In brief, NA absorbed from the intestine is actively converted to nicotinic acid riboside (NAR) NAPRT-dependently, then released into the circulation (Nomura, Nat Commun ’23. PMID: 38092728). Their paper reports that (1) the blood concentration of NA is much lower than that of NAR, and (2) Naprt deficiency significantly decreases the blood NAR levels in mice. These findings are critical to interpret the data presented in this paper. For example, in the culture experiments of this study, the authors added NA at a concentration of 100 µM, which is likely supraphysiological by a factor of 1000 or more in most organs. Direct fueling form the dietary NA or NA converted from Nam by gut microbiota may result in higher NA concentrations in the colon epithelium compared to the circulation. However, there is little direct evidence that NAD synthesis using NA as a substrate is active in other organs. Instead, it is questionable whether the proposed mechanism in this paper applies beyond the intestinal epithelium. Given the NA to NAR conversion, many of author’s claim in this paper remain speculative.
Besides the two major issues mentioned above, the following points require significant attention:
Figs 1-3: The authors added NA at a final concentration of 100 µM in many experiments in vitro. A theoretical basis for this concentration setting must be provided. Additionally, It would be better to present results with lower concentrations of NA for comparison.
Fig 2: The differences in PARylation and DNA damage between the parental and NAPRT-KO cells are relatively small. Therefore, add-back experiments should be conducted. Alternatively, experiments with multiple KO clones should be performed. Additionally, gH2AX levels should be examined by WB for a clearer comparison.
Fig 3: The NAD levels in various organs of Naprt-KO mice under steady-state conditions (without Nam load) should be reported.
Fig 4: The reason for administering additional NA through drinking water, given that NA is already provided in the dietary chow, should be clarified. Panels C-E are underwhelming, and most of them could be moved to supplementary items.
Fig 6G: The experiment appears to be very important, but the method section lacks essential details. Were comparisons made using littermates? Were events (e.g., mortality) monitored up to the time of inspection at 24 months? These are critical details for interpreting the data. Moreover, the results should be presented separately for male and female mice.
The following statements appear overly speculative or exaggerated:
Line 160-1: “suggesting that NAD pool maintained by … … DNA repair.”
Line 185: “in gut epithelial cells”
Line 186-8: “despite accumulation of more severe DNA … … the surviving cells.”
Line 213: “NAPRT-mediated deamidated NAD … … all tested tissues.”
Line 218-20: “deamidated biosynthesis is a major route of … … and lung.”
Line 296: “NAPRT deficiency is associated with an increased sensitivity to IBD.”
Line 377: “NAPRT is believed to be oncogenic.”
Line 394-5: “These results indicate that … … in both mice and humans.”
The reasoning behind the statements in lines 381-8 and lines 401-3 is difficult to follow.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The study by Wu et al. explores how the Preiss-Handler pathway in NAD biosynthesis, mediated by NAPRT, impacts NAD metabolism, DNA repair, and tumorigenesis in the gut. Key findings highlight the role of NAPRT in sustaining NAD levels across tissues such as the liver, colon, and pancreas, and the consequences of NAPRT deficiency on NAD synthesis and tissue vulnerability to NAD-depleting stress.
In NAPRT KO mice, NAD synthesis is significantly compromised under DNA damage conditions, like those induced by AOM treatment, leading to inadequate metabolic and DNA repair responses, heightened inflammation, and increased gut cell damage. This dysfunction predisposes NAPRT KO mice to more severe colitis and tumorigenesis, resulting in a higher tumor burden, advanced adenomas, and upregulated inflammatory genes, underscoring the critical function of NAPRT-mediated NAD synthesis in safeguarding gut tissue from inflammation and cancer progression.
This is a very well written paper, that provides important insights into the role of the Preiss-Handler pathway in NAD biosynthesis, particularly in the context of NAPRT and its impact on DNA repair and tumorigenesis. However, it lacks novelty in certain aspects, as highlighted in major concerns, particularly point 5. The pioneering study on the role of NAD+ in tumorigenesis by Tummala et al. (2014) as well as the controversial work by Lee et al. (2022) should be cited, discussed, and integrated into the context of the manuscript, supported by experimental evidence. Additionally, several key issues outlined below need to be addressed before this manuscript is considered suitable for publication.Once these issues are addressed, this manuscript could make a valuable contribution to the field.
Major concerns
1. The connection between NAD+ depletion and DNA damage is well-established, as shown in pivotal studies like Tummala et al. (2014) and Gomes et al. (2016), whose papers have not been cited but should. However, in their study, authors should mechanistically provide more insights into how NAPRT KO leads to DNA damage. This could result from decreased PARP activity, inhibition of Sirtuins, reduced dNTP synthesis, or perturbation in alkylation routes, all pathways where NAD+ plays a crucial role. To clarify this, the authors should measure the activities of PARP, Sirtuins, and dNTP synthesis in the NAPRT KO context. These assays would provide insight into the specific mechanisms by which NAD+ depletion leads to genotoxic stress and tumorigenesis in their model. Furthermore, performing rescue experiments, such as supplementing precursors to restore NAD+ levels or enhancing activity in the affected pathways, would significantly strengthen the study’s conclusions regarding the role of NAD+ metabolism in DNA damage and cancer progression. Rescue experiments with dNTPs, or using PARP inhibitors are also requested.
2. A key concern is that while NAMPT depletion results in cell death, NAPRT KO does not induce such effects, in particular because the medium is supplemented with NAM. Likewise, NAPRT KO mice develop normally without obvious phenotypes, whereas NAMPT KO mice are embryonically lethal. The authors conclude that the deamidated NAD biosynthesis pathway is non-essential for survival, development, or normal cellular function. However, the underlying reason for this disparity remains unclear. Are NAD+ levels significantly more reduced to be completely abolished in NAMPT KO compared to NAPRT KO, thereby leading to extensive DNA damage, cell death, and catastrophic outcomes in NAMPT KO but not in NAPRT KO? Could it be that NAD+ depletion is less severe in NAPRT KO, allowing partial compensation through NAD+ synthesis from tryptophan catabolism? Notably QPRT is expressed in human colons and therefore this pathway might still be active despite the enzymes are not highly expressed in mice. Resolving these questions is crucial, and the study would benefit from comparative NAD+ quantification between NAMPT and NAPRT KO models, along with an analysis of compensatory metabolic pathways.
3. The authors claim that their scRNA-seq analysis reveals distinct cell-type expression patterns for NAMPT and NAPRT in the small intestine and colon, with NAMPT being ubiquitously expressed across all cell types, particularly in gut immune cells, while NAPRT is relatively enriched in the epithelial compartments (Figure 1A and S1B). However, this is not entirely accurate, as NAPRT also appears to be expressed in immune cells. Thus, a complete NAPRT knockout could indeed affect NAD+ levels in immune cells, potentially impacting their functional role in reducing tumorigenesis. A conditional knockout mouse model would have been a more suitable approach to target specific cell types for this study. By restricting the NAPRT knockout to particular tissues or cell types, the authors could better assess the cell-type-specific effects of NAD+ depletion on tumorigenesis. Alternatively, the authors could utilize a xenograft or patient-derived xenograft model (that will give some clinicl relevance to the study), comparing NAPRT knockout with NAMPT knockout, to assess the tumor-inducing potential in immunodeficient mice.
4. In line with the previous comment, the authors should provide a more comprehensive explanation of their results addressing inflammation, in particular when using the DSS-induced colitis models. Reduction of NAD+ levels in their Naprt KO model induces DNA damage and this is well-known to be linked to tumour formation, especially in epithelial cells, but the connection between the reduction of NAD+ levels with inflammation is not clear. Why the reduction of NAD+ levels leads to more inflammation? Which cells contribute to this enhanced sensitivity in their KO mice? Which are the cellular pathways important for this process? Perhaps an immune cell characterization in the presence of DSS in NAPRT KO mice should be provided via scRNA seq of isolated CD45+ cells. The conditional KO mouse model would have solved these questions. We do understand that this is not possible at this stage, but authors could explored alternative experiments such as PDX or/and xenografts studies in immunodeficient mice to circumvent this.
5. A rescue experiment using nicotinamide riboside (NR) both in vitro (Figure 1) and in vivo to counteract the effects of NAPRT depletion on tumorigenesis would be highly valuable. For tumorigenesis, NR should be implemented in prevention and in therapy once tumors are formed to better understand the pro- or anti-tumorigenic effects of NAPRT KO. This experiment could provide direct evidence for the potential therapeutic role of NR in restoring NAD+ levels and mitigating the negative effects of NAD+ depletion on DNA repair, inflammation, and tumorigenesis. Including such data would significantly strengthen the manuscript by demonstrating the feasibility of NR as a potential intervention for restoring NAD+ homeostasis and reducing cancer progression in the context of NAPRT deficiency.
6. While this study introduces the first NAPRT KO mouse model to explore the role of the Preiss-Handler pathway in tumorigenesis, the concept of NAD+ depletion in DNA damage and cancer is not novel. The authors overlook the foundational work by Tummala et al., published in Cancer Cell in 2014, which first demonstrated the significance of NAD+ depletion in tumorigenesis. Additionally, the study by Lee et al., published in Cancer Discovery in 2022, has been ignored. In their work, the authors showed that APC-deficient colorectal cancer models were susceptible to TDO2 depletion or pharmacological inhibition, leading to NAD+ depletion, impaired cancer cell proliferation, and enhanced antitumor immune responses. These important studies should be cited, discussed, and integrated into the context of the current manuscript through experimental evidence. One possible explanation to the study of Lee et al. is that since APC deletion drives cell proliferation, cells might rely on increased NAD+ from de novo synthesis to initiate DNA synthesis and repair pathways. Without the support of the NAPRT-NAD+ arm, APC-deleted cells may not survive. Therefore, it is crucial to measure NAD+ levels under different conditions in order to determine how the depletion of NAPRT affects cellular NAD+ metabolism, especially in the context of APC deletion. This would help clarify whether NAPRT-mediated NAD+ synthesis is essential for the survival and function of APC-deleted cells and further elucidate the role of NAD+ in DNA repair and cell survival under genotoxic stress.
7. Figure 2D is difficult to understand, and the data interpretation lacks clarity. The authors claim that STF treatment sensitizes cells to MMS-induced cell death by comparing WT MMS+STF to WT MMS alone. However, when discussing the inactivation of deamidated synthesis in KO cells, the authors compare KO MMS to WT MMS instead, which seems inconsistent. According to Figure 2C, KO cells appear to have more DNA damage; therefore, in Figure 2D, MMS treatment alone would be expected to result in fewer colonies in KO cells compared to WT, but this outcome is not shown. Furthermore, if the comparison in KO cells were done similarly to WT cells—that is, MMS+STF vs. MMS alone—a similar observation (fewer colonies with STF treatment) would likely emerge. The precise methodology of this experiment, particularly the comparisons drawn between groups, needs more explanation.
Minor points
1. Some data described in the text is not shown in the figures (e.g. Figure 1 is missing to show cell morphology and proliferation rates).
2. Some panels of the figures are not even mentioned in the text (e.g. Figure 2A). All data shown in the figures must be discussed.
3. Figure legends contain explanations already present in the results section. They should be more descriptive and summarized.
4. Full uncut immunoblots should not be added in the supplementary figures (Fig. S1D, Fig. S2B).
5. In lines 141-142, the authors claim that ‘’ NAPRT deficiency impairs cellular metabolism and increases the sensitivity of gut epithelial cells to NAMPT inhibition induced NAD depletion and subsequence cell death’’. However, the authors should provide an experiment that shows that cell death occurs such as Brdu incorporation or stainings for apoptotic markers.
6. The authors should consider changing the title of the manuscript since it does not align with the findings shown.
7. Figure 3D, quantify the number of organoids
8. The authors explain the observed phenotypes due to the accumulation of DNA damage due to NAD+ depletion. Therefore, DNA damage measures are key to support their conclusions. In this regard, authors rely on yH2AX staining quantified by intensity/cell. The use of additional DNA markers for DNA damage, beyond yH2AX, should be also included to further corroborate their results. In addition, measure of DNA damage in their NARPT KO aged mice is also requested.
9. The authors should show the activation of DNA repair pathways in gut epithelial cells upon DNA damage.
10. Microbiome or diet are the source of NA is their study? The relevance of the microbiome could be explored via antibiotics treatment to get insights into its role.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The manuscript by Xiaoyue and colleagues “NAPRT-mediated deamidated NAD biosynthesis enhances tissue resiliency and suppresses tumorigenesis,” aims to investigate the tumour suppressing roles of the deamidated arm of NAD biosynthesis. To achieve that, they constructed NAPRT gene knock-out models and assess their effects using both in vitro (CRC119 cell lines and colonic organoids) and in vivo (mouse) systems. Here they found that removal of NAPRT gene altered metabolism such as glycolysis, increased DNA damage, impaired PARP activity, heightened sensitivity to inflammatory stress, and susceptibility to tumorigenesis in mouse models. Furthermore, reduced NAPRT expression correlates with poor prognosis in stage 1, not stage 3 and 4, CRC patients.
The manuscript is well-written, and the analyses are thorough and comprehensive. In my view, the findings presented in this manuscript are valuable and provide some insights into the mechanisms underlying colorectal cancer (CRC) development. Additionally, these insight may also extend to understanding precancerous conditions, such as polyps, offering a foundation for further research in this area.
However, I have a few comments that I hope the authors will address to strengthen the manuscript further:
1. The authors focus their study on gut, but occasionally deviate and discuss NAPRT expression in other organs without clear purpose or sufficient discussion, which may confuse the reader. For example, it is not clear why the author show NAD metabolites in liver instead of colon in figure 3A?
2. For NAPRT/NAPRT expression in humans (Fig. 1A or Fig. 6I), it would be helpful to stratify the data based on previously published transcriptomic subtypes, such as CMS (https://doi.org/10.1038/nm.3967), IMF (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41588-022-01100-4), or MSI/MSS, to provide a more detailed understanding.
3. It would also be interesting to investigate whether there is any dysregulation of NAPRT in the polyps. The authors could consider utilizing previously published polyp datasets, such as those from Chen et al. (Cell, Volume 184, Issue 26, 6262 - 6280.e26) or Becker et al. (Nat Genet 54, 985–995 (2022)), to explore this further.
4. The mechanism behind the increase in NA following NAM feeding in the mouse model is unclear. The authors suggest that gut bacteria may convert dietary NAM to NA, but a similar increase in NA was also observed in other organs (Fig. 3C). Further explanation are needed.
5. It is unclear why NA was used as the substrate in the in vitro experiments, while NAM was used in the in vivo studies. The authors may consider using NAM as the substrate in the in vitro system as well, which could also help address my previous question (point 4).
6. Figure 4A, why NA level was decreased in KO mice after AOM treatment?
7. Figure 4C:
a. Why was the group highlighted in the black box below are not discussed? This group appears to include genes that are highly expressed in both WT and KO at 12 hours but downregulated in WT at 48 hours.
b. It would also be interesting to compare genes within the group across different time points (e.g., WT0 vs. WT12 vs. WT48) and then examine which pathways are altered in the KO
8. Figure 5H: The author write in line 330-333 that NAMPT, NAPRT and NADSYN1 are differentially altered in IBD. However, figure 5H clearly shown only NAMPT are differentially altered. This results actually contradict their conclusion that "NAPRT deficiency is associate with increased sensitivity to IBD". Better explanation and support are needed.
a. The author may also be interested in checking the NAPRT expression in colon instead of intestine (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-0992-y).
9. Figure 6I: The authors state in lines 387-388 that “TCGA datasets showed that the mRNA levels of NAPRT are reduced in a significant proportion of tumors,” which is inaccurate. Figure 6I shows that, in COAD, only 40% of patients show a reduction in NAPRT, while another 40% actually show an increase. This discrepancy is even more pronounced in the LUAD and LUSC datasets, where a larger proportion of patients exhibit increased NAPRT expression. This contradicts the authors' claim that reduced deamidated NAD biosynthesis is associated with tumorigenesis in both mice and humans (lines 394-395). A better explanation and additional support for this discrepancy are needed.
10. The figure legends could be improved. Ex: it is unclear what is M+2, M+3, and M+4 in figure 3A and what is 0.5,1,1.5, and 2 in figure 5A means.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Thanks for this insightful comment. We agree with the reviewer that we don’t have a clear mechanistic understanding why cancer patients with low NAPRT-low tumors have worse prognosis than patients with NAPRT-high tumors. To address the reviewer’s concern, we deleted the sentence “This observation in CRC supports the notion that NAPRT-mediated deamidated NAD biosynthesis is important for DNA repair, thereby suppressing tumor initiation” from the last paragraph of the Results section. We also modified the Discussion section and toned down the link of NAPRT and DNA repair in human patients.
Another major issue is that this study overlooks recent important findings on systemic NA metabolism. In brief, NA absorbed from the intestine is actively converted to nicotinic acid riboside (NAR) NAPRT-dependently, then released into the circulation (Nomura, Nat Commun ’23. PMID: 38092728). Their paper reports that (1) the blood concentration of NA is much lower than that of NAR, and (2) Naprt deficiency significantly decreases the blood NAR levels in mice. These findings are critical to interpret the data presented in this paper. For example, in the culture experiments of this study, the authors added NA at a concentration of 100 µM, which is likely supraphysiological by a factor of 1000 or more in most organs. Direct fueling form the dietary NA or NA converted from Nam by gut microbiota may result in higher NA concentrations in the colon epithelium compared to the circulation. However, there is little direct evidence that NAD synthesis using NA as a substrate is active in other organs. Instead, it is questionable whether the proposed mechanism in this paper applies beyond the intestinal epithelium. Given the NA to NAR conversion, many of author’s claim in this paper remain speculative.
If we understood the argument here correctly, the reviewer believed that based on the referenced study, NAR but NA is the major circulating deamidated NAD precursor after dietary supplementation of NA/NAM. Therefore, the reduced NAD synthesis we observed in organs other than the colon epithelium in NAPRT KO mice was due to reduced circulating NAR released from the colon, rather than deletion of NAPRT in these organs. Thereby, the reviewer concluded that “there is little direct evidence that NAD synthesis using NA as a substrate is active in other organs”.
This argument would hold true if only the data from the referenced paper were considered.
However, our findings from the current study, along with those from a previous study, contradict this interpretation. First, our finding that NA was massively accumulated in all tested NAPRT KO mouse tissues (Figure 3C, S3F, and S3G) provided direct evidence that NAD synthesis using NA as a substrate is active in all these tissues. Moreover, the observation that robust NAAD and NAD biosynthesis in WT mice occurred without significant accumulation of NA, even at the earliest time point examined (except for the colon) (Figure 3C, NA), indicating that NAPRT-mediated NA assimilation is swift and highly efficient. Second, in our prior study 1, we analyzed systemic NAM/NR/NA/NAR metabolism. As shown in Figure 6D and Figure S5G of that paper, following oral NAM gavage, NAMN was the most abundant deamidated NAD precursor in both portal blood (12 pmol/mg) and inferior vena cava blood (8 pmol/mg), compared to 1.5 pmol/mg NA and 0.3 pmol/mg NR in inferior vena cava blood (Figure R1). Thus, in our experimental system, NAR is not the major circulating deamidated precursor. Yet despite the presence of various circulating deamidated precursors, NA accumulated in KO tissues beyond the intestinal epithelium, strongly indicating that NA serves as a main source for deamidated NAD biosynthesis in these tissues.
For the criticism on the concentration of NA we used in the cell culture system, please see our response below.
Besides the two major issues mentioned above, the following points require significant attention:
Figs 1-3: The authors added NA at a final concentration of 100 µM in many experiments in vitro. A theoretical basis for this concentration setting must be provided. Additionally, It would be better to present results with lower concentrations of NA for comparison.
Indeed, the concentration of NA in the serum of mice on regular chow diet is around 1 µM NA 1. However, it has been reported that this concentration goes up to 50-100 µM 8 hours after oral gavage with 500 mg/kg NR 2. Please note that we and others have shown that NR is degraded in the gut to NAM, which is then deamidated by the gut microbiota to NA 1, 2. Moreover, we have previously showed that in the colon, the NA concentration reaches 400 µM after gavage with 80 mg/kg NAM 1. Thus, 100 µM of NA in our culture system is well within the physiological range after supplementation with NAD boosting supplements.
To further address the reviewer’s concern, we performed a dose-response experiment, which revealed a biphasic response of NAD levels to increasing NA concentrations with 12.5-25 µM NA resulting in maximal increase in cellular NAD (Figure S2D). We then repeated the DNA damage experiment shown in Figure 2C, but now using 20 µM instead of 100 uM NA. We confirmed that NAPRT KO cells also have higher basal and MMS-induced DNA damage in the presence of this lower NA concentration (Figure S2E and new Figure 2B, see below).
Fig 2: The differences in PARylation and DNA damage between the parental and NAPRT-KO cells are relatively small. Therefore, add-back experiments should be conducted.
As suggested by the reviewer, we performed add-back experiments by transiently overexpressing NAPRT in two independent NAPRT KO clones. Cells were then treated with MMS for 1 hour and co-stained for NAPRT and gH2AX. As shown in Figure S2F and 2D, in both clones DNA damage was significantly lower in NAPRT-positive than in NAPRT-negative cells, confirming the genuine role of NAPRT in DNA repair.
Alternatively, experiments with multiple KO clones should be performed. Additionally, gH2AX levels should be examined by WB for a clearer comparison.
The WT and NAPRT KO cells we used in the original Figure 2 are mixture of two independent clones each. We apologize that we forgot to mention this in the Methods section. Additionally, the PARylation results in Figure S2B are from two independent clones.
To further address the reviewer’s concern, we optimized the timeframe of MMS treatment and analyzed Mono-ADP-ribosylation (MARylation) and gH2AX by western blotting in two independent KO clones separately. Cells were supplemented with 20 µM NA to address reviewer’s request to repeat some experiments with a lower NA concentration. Similar to our results on PARylation (Figure S2B and S2C), auto MARylation of PARP1 (upper band) and MARylation of histones (lower band), which was recently shown to be important for efficient DNA repair 3, were less induced in both KO clones (Figure 2B), demonstrating reduced induction of PARP activity. The results further confirmed that NAPRT KO cells have increased gH2AX after MMS treatment in both KO clones, providing an additional piece of clear evidence that NAPRT KO cells have defective DNA repair thereby accumulating DNA damage after MMS treatment.
Please note that in the revision, the new MARylation and gH2AX results are shown in new Figure 2B, and the original PARylation data are moved into supplementary figures as Figure S2C.
Fig 3: The NAD levels in various organs of Naprt-KO mice under steady-state conditions (without Nam load) should be reported.
We added a new Figure S3D showing that without dietary supplementation of NAD precursors, the steady-state tissue NAD levels were normal in all tested tissues of NAPRT KO mice. As stated in our response to the next point, we believe this is due to compensation from amidated and/or de novo pathways.
Fig 4: The reason for administering additional NA through drinking water, given that NA is already provided in the dietary chow, should be clarified.
The reason why we supplemented experimental mice with NA in this experiment is because the chow diet (NIH-31) in our animal facility contains a very low level of NA (0.0083%) but a high level of Trp (0.20%), the precursor for de novo NAD biosynthesis. Given that hepatocytes, which have high expression of Qprt (Figure S1B), are the main producers of circulating NAM from NAD (>95% of total circulating NAM) and that circulating NAM serves as the primary NAD precursor for most tissues in vivo 4, it is likely that hepatic de novo NAD biosynthesis from Trp compensated for the defective deamidated NAD synthesis in NAPRT KO mice fed the chow diet. Additionally, although the expression of Qprt in mouse intestinal epithelial cells is very low under normal conditions (Figure 1A), we were concerned that it might be activated by increased NAD consumption upon AOM-induced DNA damage, potentially masking the deficiency caused by NAPRT deletion. We therefore decided to supplement NA to increase the dependence of experimental mice on the deamidated pathway.
Panels C-E are underwhelming, and most of them could be moved to supplementary items.
We agree with the reviewer, therefore moved Figure 4E into Figure S5D.
Fig 6G: The experiment appears to be very important, but the method section lacks essential details. Were comparisons made using littermates? Were events (e.g., mortality) monitored up to the time of inspection at 24 months? These are critical details for interpreting the data.
The WT and NAPRT KO mice were originally littermates. After being backcrossed into the C57BL/6J background for four generations, they were bred separately within each genotype to produce sufficient experimental animals within the available space for this study.
For two cohorts of mice analyzed in this specific experiment, their health status and mortality were regularly monitored by the institute veterinary medicine staff during the two-year period of the study. But unfortunately, due to the renovation of the animal facility during this period, they were transferred multiple times between rooms, and we were not able to locate their health status and mortality records. The only data we have for these two cohorts is that at the time of inspection at 24 months, 6 out of 17 WT and 12 out 17 KO female mice were removed/lost, and 11 out 23 WT and 8 out of 27 KO male mice were removed/lost due to health issues/mortality. This result suggests that female NAPRT KO mice may have increased mortality. Indeed, analyzing another two ongoing independent aging cohorts confirmed that female but not male NAPRT KO mice had significantly reduced symptom-free survival compared with age-matched WT females (new Figure 7G). Among those females removed/lost from the aging cohort, 5 out 16 KO were due to visible large abdominal mass or rectal prolapse, whereas none of 6 removed/lost WT displayed these tumor-related symptoms.
Moreover, the results should be presented separately for male and female mice.
Thanks for the suggestion. We re-graphed the original tumor incidence data and presented male and female mice separately and showed them in new Figure 7H.
The following statements appear overly speculative or exaggerated:
Line 160-1: “suggesting that NAD pool maintained by … … DNA repair.”
This statement was deleted in the revision.
Line 185: “in gut epithelial cells”
Deleted in the revision.
Line 186-8: “despite accumulation of more severe DNA … … the surviving cells.”
We hope that our new data will convince the reviewer that DNA damage is indeed more severe in NAPRT KO cells. We also now provide additional evidence that a “comparable fraction of NAPRT-deficient gut epithelial cells survives the stress” using Cell-titer GLO assay after 72 hours of continuous MMS treatment (Figure 2F, ATP (72 hours)). We believe that we were careful enough at this early point in the paper to qualify our hypothesis that increased DNA damage coupled with equal cell survival may be “potentially leading to increased mutagenesis and tumorigenesis within the surviving cells.” We use this hypothesis as a setup for the following cancer-related experiments and analyses. We are glad that the Reviewer found our results on increased tumorigenesis in NAPRT KO mice in 3 different models (AOM-DSS, APC, spontaneous aging) convincing. Since we do not provide direct evidence on increased mutagenesis, we deleted “mutagenesis” from this sentence.
Line 213: “NAPRT-mediated deamidated NAD … … all tested tissues.”
Please see our response to the second major concern. This is an accurate statement.
Line 218-20: “deamidated biosynthesis is a major route of … … and lung.”
Please see our response to the second major concern. This is an accurate statement.
Line 296: “NAPRT deficiency is associated with an increased sensitivity to IBD.”
We changed the title of this section to “NAPRT deficiency is associated with an increased sensitivity to DSS-induced colitis.”
Line 377: “NAPRT is believed to be oncogenic.”
This statement was changed into “NAPRT is found to be frequently amplified and/or overexpressed in various human cancer types and its knockdown slowed growth of xenograft tumors, suggesting tumor-promoting role of this gene 5, 6.”
Line 394-5: “These results indicate that … … in both mice and humans.”
This statement was deleted in the revision.
The reasoning behind the statements in lines 381-8 and lines 401-3 is difficult to follow.
We modified the statement in lines 381-8 into “In support of this hypothesis, AOM/DSS-induced tumorigenesis in WT mice was coupled with reduced expression of key deamidated NAD biosynthesis genes (Figure 8A). Compared to normal colon tissues from age- and gender-matched untreated mice, tumor adjacent colon tissues from AOM/DSS treated WT mice had significantly reduced expression of both Naprt and Nadsyn but not Nampt (Figure 8A, Adjacent vs Normal). The mRNA levels of these two key deamidated NAD biosynthesis enzymes were further reduced in AOM/DSS-induced tumors (Figure 8A, Tumor vs Adjacent).”
The statement in lines 401-3 was deleted.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This manuscript is a revised version of a paper I previously reviewed. In this revision, several issues have been addressed and improved. However, I believe there remain critical concerns, particularly regarding aspects of systemic nicotinic acid (NA) metabolism, that require further revision.
Major points
1. In my previous review, I pointed out that there is a Nat Commun paper (Nomura M, PMID: 38092728) demonstrating that NA is converted to NAR in a NAPRT-dependent manner. During this revision period, an additional study reported NA-to-NAR conversion in mice (Song WS, Cell Metab ’25, PMID: 40315855). Thus, two independent groups have now shown that NA can be converted to NAR. Nevertheless, the present manuscript does not mention or consider this conversion pathway at all. I believe this omission constitutes a significant limitation.
2. The authors state that the NA concentration used in the in vitro experiments (100 uM) is comparable to the peak serum concentration following NAD booster administration, as reported in the previous study (Chellappa K, Cell Metab ’22, PMID: 36476934). While this is factually correct, the study also reported that steady-state levels of NA (in the absence of NR administration) are very low. Omitting this point could lead readers to overestimate physiological NA concentrations.
3. To allow for a more accurate and reliable interpretation of the metabolic data presented in this study, I strongly recommend that the authors include, at a minimum, plasma or serum (not whole blood) concentrations of NAD-related metabolites in WT and Naprt-KO mice, both at both at baseline (prior to NA administration) and at multiple time points following NA administration. Blood sampling should preferably be performed from the systemic circulation, rather than the portal vein, to better reflect whole-body metabolism. In this context, blood collection from the right ventricle is considered the most appropriate.
Minor points.
4. In Figures 1 and 2, the in vitro experiments were conducted using only one colorectal cancer cell line, CRC119. The authors should be more cautious in generalizing the results to normal “gut epithelial cells” as a whole. In addition, more information about CRC119 should be provided in the Methods section; at present, even the species is not indicated.
5. In Figure 2D, the results of the add-back experiment are not clear. Such experiments should be performed using a stable expression system, rather than transient transfection.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
At the outset, I was indeed very positive about this manuscript, under the condition that my initial comments were thoroughly addressed. While the paper remains a very well-written and insightful contribution, providing important advances on the role of the Preiss–Handler pathway in NAD biosynthesis, particularly the function of NAPRT in DNA repair and tumorigenesis, it is concerning that some of my key points appear to have been overlooked.
Several other key issues outlined below remain unaddressed. I strongly recommend that these be carefully revised and clarified before the manuscript can be considered suitable for publication. If adequately addressed, this work could indeed represent a valuable contribution to the field.
Point 1
In particular, as highlighted in my Major Concern, the pioneering study by Tummala et al. (2014) on the role of NAD⁺ in tumorigenesis, along with the more recent and controversial work by Lee et al. (2022), should be not only cited—which the authors have done—but also properly discussed and integrated into the conceptual framework of the manuscript. These citations currently lack critical engagement.
I respectfully disagree with the response provided to Comment 1. The authors argue that their study is mechanistically distinct from the work of Tummala et al. and Gomes et al., both of which demonstrated that NAD⁺ depletion leads to DNA damage, likely through PARP inactivation or reduced dNTP synthesis. While the authors emphasize that their study centers on NAPRT and its role in DNA repair, they also conclude that NAPRT knockout cells, which have compromised NAD⁺ levels, exhibit defective DNA repair and accumulate DNA damage upon MMS treatment.
In my view, the underlying message of these studies remains fundamentally aligned. Therefore, a proper and critical discussion of these prior findings is necessary. Without it, the current manuscript falls short in demonstrating sufficient novelty.
Mechanistic insights into how NAPRT deficiency leads to DNA damage remain insufficiently resolved. Although the authors now demonstrate reduced PARylation and MARylation in NAPRT KO cells, this evidence essentially confirms the role of PARP in their phenotype, thereby aligning their study more closely with previously published findings. Similarly, while SIRT1's role remains unclear in their system, and dNTP synthesis appears largely unaffected. As established in seminal studies such as Tummala et al. (2014) and Gomes et al. (2016), NAD⁺ depletion can lead to DNA damage through several converging pathways, including PARP inactivation, Sirtuin inhibition, and reduced dNTP synthesis, all of which are potentially relevant in this context. These studies should be properly cited and integrated into the manuscript’s conceptual framework.
Therefore, I respectfully maintain that the manuscript would benefit from a more rigorous and integrative discussion acknowledging how their findings intersect with existing knowledge and litteratire. The notion that NAPRT-derived NAD⁺ is essential for DNA repair in gut epithelial cells is interesting; however, the message conveyed converges with previously published observations about NAD⁺ depletion and genome instability. This convergence must be transparently acknowledged and discussed to better contextualize the contribution of this work and to address concerns around novelty.
It is unclear why the authors have chosen to omit citation and discussion of previous pioneering studies that have significantly shaped the understanding of NAD⁺ metabolism and its role in DNA damage and tumorigenesis.
Point 2
The authors fairly replied to this point: Orally administered NR and NMN are largely converted by gut microbiota into nicotinic acid (NA), which then enters the Preiss-Handler pathway requiring NAPRT for NAD⁺ synthesis. In NAPRT knockout (KO) models, this pathway is disrupted, preventing NAD⁺ restoration from NR/NMN, as seen in both in vitro (e.g., CRC119 cells) and in vivo studies.
Despite this, NR and NMN remain widely used because, in organisms with functional NAPRT and normal gut microbiota, they effectively boost NAD⁺ levels and provide physiological benefits. Thus, the efficacy of NR/NMN depends on the presence of NAPRT and highlights the critical role of the Preiss-Handler pathway in their metabolism.
Yet, dietary levels of tryptophan may be sufficient to compensate for NAPRT deficiency in many tissues. This has not been tested. A rescue experiment can still be important.
Point 3
This is justified by the authors stating, “We agree that conditional NAPRT KO in different cell types would be more informative. However, as the reviewer noted here, such studies are beyond the scope of the current revision.”
This is inaccurate; the reviewer never claimed it was beyond the scope but explicitly requested this experiment. Nevertheless, the xenograft studies presented do not fully support the paper’s conclusions, and conditional KO mouse models would be important to address this gap.
Other important points
I regret to note that γH2AX, the standard marker for DNA damage, has not been successfully demonstrated in this study, despite its widespread and well-established use in numerous publications. It is unclear why evidence of DNA damage is not provided or visible here.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: The authors have addressed all my concern

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
To answer the reviewer’s question about whether NA or NAR is the main circulating deamidated NAD precursor beyond the intestinal epithelium during the first revision, we provided evidence that NA is the main source for deamidated NAD biosynthesis in various tested mouse tissues. However, we did not realize that the reviewer would also like to see our measurement on the conversion of NA to NAR. We apologize for the oversight.
To address this concern as well as Point #3, we orally gavaged D4-labeled NA into WT and NAPRT KO mice, then followed the kinetics of NA, NAR, and NAM in systemic plasma. As shown in the new Figure S3I, the baseline concentration of NA (M+0) in plasma of mice under the regular chow diet, which was reported to be around 1 µM by Chellappa et al. 1, was below the detection limit of our platform (1-2 µM). One hour after oral gavage of D4-NA at 80 mg/Kg, plasma NA levels rose to 278±73 µM in WT and 824±217 µM in KO mice, indicating reduced NA utilization in NAPRT KO mice.
NA levels dropped below the detection limit by three hours after gavage (Figure S3I, NA).
Supporting the reviewer’s note that NA can be converted into NAR in an NAPRT-dependent manner 2, we observed a significant increase in plasma NAR levels (from 0.028± 0.007 µM to 0.202± 0.007 µM) in WT mice one hour post-gavage, and this increase was almost completely abolished in KO mice (Figure S3I, NAR). Additionally, D4-NA gavage elevated plasma levels of both M+0 and M+3 NAM, peaking between 1- 3 hours in WT but not in KO mice (Figure S3I, NAM), suggesting increased NAD consumption following NA-induced NAD boosting in WT mice.
Because the peak NAR concentration we observed in WT mice (~0.2 µM) is much lower than levels (1-2 µM) reported by recent studies 2, 3, we repeated the experiment using 400 mg/Kg D4-NA as in Song et al. 3. Even then, plasma NAR levels remained below 0.3 µM three hours after gavage, in contrast to 540 µM of NA (Figure S3I, right panels).
2. The authors state that the NA concentration used in the in vitro experiments (100 uM) is comparable to the peak serum concentration following NAD booster administration, as reported in the previous study (Chellappa K, Cell Metab ’22, PMID: 36476934). While this is factually correct, the study also reported that steady-state levels of NA (in the absence of NR administration) are very low. Omitting this point could lead readers to overestimate physiological NA concentrations.
The reviewer is correct that the baseline concentration of NA in plasma of mice under the regular chow diet without supplementation was reported to be around 1 µM by Chellappa et al. 1. We agree with the reviewer that even the reduced concentration of 20 µM NA, which we used in the first revision to address this criticism, is still significantly higher than 1 µM. In response to this point, we used 1 µM NA in the new NAPRT add-back MMS experiment requested in point 5.
As shown in new Figure 2E, the higher DNA damage in NAPRT KO cells was also observed with this physiologically relevant NA concentration. Stable re-expression of HA-mNAPRT rescued this defect, confirming the genuine role of NAPRT in DNA repair. Our results further suggest that NAPRT-mediated NAD synthesis may be important for maintenance of homeostatic DNA repair.
3. To allow for a more accurate and reliable interpretation of the metabolic data presented in this study, I strongly recommend that the authors include, at a minimum, plasma or serum (not whole blood) concentrations of NAD-related metabolites in WT and Naprt-KO mice, both at both at baseline (prior to NA administration) and at multiple time points following NA administration. Blood sampling should preferably be performed from the systemic circulation, rather than the portal vein, to better reflect whole-body metabolism. In this context, blood collection from the right ventricle is considered the most appropriate.
We performed the experiment requested by the reviewer and the new data are included in new Figure S3I (please see our response to Point #1).
Minor points.
4. In Figures 1 and 2, the in vitro experiments were conducted using only one colorectal cancer cell line, CRC119. The authors should be more cautious in generalizing the results to normal “gut epithelial cells” as a whole.
In addition to CRC119 cancer line data, the conclusion about the increased sensitivity of NAPRT KO to DNA damage is based on increased gH2Ax staining of normal gut epithelial cells before and after in-vivo AOM treatment of mice (Figure 4D). However, as requested by the reviewer, since our mechanistic studies were performed in CRC119 cells and presented on a separate figure than the in vivo data, we changed “NAPRT-deficient gut epithelial cells” to “NAPRT-deficient cells“ when describing the results on Figure 2.
In addition, more information about CRC119 should be provided in the Methods section; at present, even the species is not indicated.
We did mention in the main text (page 7) that CRC119 is a human colon cancer cell line. We provided a reference to the paper describing the derivation of this cell line 4 and added this information also in the method section in this revision.
5. In Figure 2D, the results of the add-back experiment are not clear. Such experiments should be performed using a stable expression system, rather than transient transfection.
Per the reviewer’s request, we stably expressed HA-mNAPRT in KO cells and performed MMS experiment using a more physiological 1 µM NA concentration in response to Point #2. The new data are shown in new Figure 2E (please see our response to Point #2).
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Point 1
We apologize that we did not provide a rigorous and integrative discussion to acknowledge previous pioneering studies on NAD, DNA damage, and tumorigenesis in our first revision. In this revision, we added the following paragraph in the Discussion section:
“The importance of NAD in supporting DNA repair and maintaining genome stability has been well-established in the literature (reviewed in 5, 6). Consistently, pathological conditions that lead to NAD depletion, such as aging, high-fat diet feeding, and oncogenic gene expression, have been reported to increase DNA damage and promote tumorigenesis through various NAD-dependent mechanisms, including PARP inactivation, sirtuin inhibition, and reduced dNTP synthesis. For instance, a seminal study by Tummala et al. showed that in hepatocytes, suppression of the de novo NAD biosynthesis pathway by expression of an oncogene unconventional prefoldin RPB5 interactor (URI) leads to reduced cellular NAD levels and increased DNA damage at early stages of tumorigenesis possibly by inhibition of PARP 7. Restoration of hepatic NAD pool with NR supplementation prevents DNA damage and tumor formation 7. In a following-up study, Gomes et al. reported that URI-induced inhibition of de novo NAD biosynthesis and subsequent DNA damage also trigger hepatic T cell infiltration and increase IL-17A production, which further promotes non-alcoholic steatohepatitis and hepatocellular carcinoma 8. These defects could also be abolished by dietary supplementation of NR 8. In the present study, by utilizing a genetic NAPRT KO model that enabled us to investigate the role of the Preiss-Handler arm of the deamidated NAD biosynthesis during tumor initiation, we demonstrated that in the gut epithelium, deficiency of this pathway impairs PARP activity and compromises DNA repair, thereby increasing susceptibility to inflammation and tumorigenesis. To our knowledge, this is the first study to identify endogenous NAPRT as a tumor suppressor rather than a tumor promoter.”
We hope this addition addressed the reviewer’s concern.
Point 2
We are sorry that we are not sure what type of “rescue” experiment the reviewer is requesting here.
If "a rescue experiment” refers to tryptophan (Trp) supplementation, we are concerned that such an experiment may not yield meaningful outcomes. The conversion of Trp to NAD is only one of several Trp metabolic fates that requires eight metabolic reactions, and the ratio of conversion is low (e.g. ~ 60:1 in humans) 9, 10. This conversion is expected to be particularly limited in the gut, where QPRT expression is minimal (Figure 1A). Indeed, in a recent report published in Cell Metabolism, Song et al. showed that Trp only boosts NAD levels in the liver and kidney 3. Since our study is focused on the gut, a rescue experiment with Trp supplementation is not feasible.
Alternatively, if the reviewer’s intention is to ask us to test whether “dietary Trp compensates for NAPRT deficiency in many tissues”, then we could potentially place NAPRT KO mice on a Trp-deficient diet so that any possible compensations from de novo NAD synthesis will be unmasked. However, the NAMPT-mediated amidated NAD salvage could very likely compensate loss of both NAPRT deficiency and inhibition of de novo pathway, masking any effects from Trp restriction. Moreover, Trp is an essential amino acid with broad roles beyond NAD synthesis, including protein biosynthesis and generation of multiple bioactive metabolites 11. It also has extensive interactions with gut microbiota and Trp-deficient diet feeding has been shown to induce intestinal inflammation and many other adverse effects 12. These NAD-independent effects would significantly complicate interpretation of any observed phenotypes.
Given these factors, we are unsure how Trp rescue and/or restriction experiments would yield interpretable or meaningful results.
Point 3
We apologize that we are not able to generate a conditional KO mouse model within a reasonable time-frame to meet this request.
In terms of the xenograft results, we respectfully disagree with the reviewer’s interpretation. As previously noted (in the first revision), using NAPRT KO mouse model, we found that impaired deamidated NAD biosynthesis in NAPRT deficient cells leads to diminished PARP activity and compromised DNA repair in response to carcinogen-induced DNA damage. This defect in DNA repair increases the rate of oncogenic mutations, thereby promoting cancer initiation. Established cancer cell lines used in the xenograft experiment, on the other hand, are not suitable to study oncogenic mutation-associated cancer initiation because they have already accumulated all the mutations needed for malignant growth. Further inhibition of DNA repair by deletion of NAPRT in these cell lines is not expected to further enhance their growth rate. It can instead decrease the growth rate of xenograft tumors due to excessive DNA damage and reduced metabolic fitness. This outcome was supported by results from our xenograft experiment as well as by previous published findings 13.
We would like to again emphasize that our study is the first to demonstrate that NAPRT can function as a tumor suppressor rather than a tumor promoter. This novel finding was made possible by our use of a newly developed genetic NAPRT KO model, which enabled us to investigate the effects of NAPRT deficiency during tumor initiation, in contrast to prior studies using xenograft models based on established cancer cell lines. In fact, our observations that NAPRT deficiency increased tumor initiation in mice but reduced tumor growth in established cancer cell lines reveal an intriguing stage-specific role of NAD in cancer: suppressing tumor initiation at early stages while supporting tumor growth and progression at later stages. We believe this finding offers valuable guidance for the development of future NAD-based strategies in cancer prevention and treatment.
Other important points
I regret to note that γH2AX, the standard marker for DNA damage, has not been successfully demonstrated in this study, despite its widespread and well-established use in numerous publications. It is unclear why evidence of DNA damage is not provided or visible here.
We are perplexed by the comment here because we believe that our data in Figures 2B, 2C, 2D, new 2E, 4D, S2E, and S2F clearly showed increased γH2AX in NAPRT KO cells and mice following genotoxic stress. Particularly, our new NAPRT add-back experiment (Figure 2E) further validates the authentic role of NAPRT in DNA repair at physiological levels of NA (1 µM) as demonstrated by higher γH2AX in KO cells and rescue of this defect by NAPRT add-back.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
I appreciate that in this revision the authors have addressed the concerns I previously raised. However, there remains one important issue that should be resolved before publication. I apologize for not noticing it earlier, but I believe it is critical for the validity of the study.
This concerns the mutant mouse line referred to as “Naprt-KO” in the manuscript. Typically, genome-editing–based gene disruption involves a frameshift mutation, which leads to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and thus a marked reduction in transcript levels. However, as the authors noted, the allele in this mouse carries an in-frame deletion of seven amino acid residues (Fig. S3A), which would not normally cause a severe decrease in mRNA levels as reported in Fig. S3B.
Although several functional studies in the paper suggest a loss of Naprt activity, it remains essential to confirm that Naprt protein is indeed absent in this mutant line. This could be demonstrated, for example, by Western blotting of tissue lysates. Such verification would clarify whether the allele truly represents a null mutation.
I am aware that the deletion may have disrupted an exon splicing enhancer (ESE), potentially leading to cryptic splicing; however, this possibility further underscores the need to verify the actual loss of Naprt protein.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Although I was initially very critical of certain experiments and aspects of the discussion, the authors have addressed all my concerns. I am satisfied with their responses and the revisions provided.
One minor point is that the authors should discuss the limitation of the study arising from the use of xenograft models, rather than the use of conditional NAPRT knockout in different cell types.
With this minor suggestion, I recommend that this paper be accepted for publication.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:

The aim of this verification qPCR is to confirm the deletion of the 21-bp in the Naprt KO cells and tissues. The sequences of these WT specific primers have already been included in Table S7 (mNAPRT genotyping-F and mNAPRT genotyping-R). We have another set of qPCR primers of mNAPRT, which are specific for Exon 1 of Naprt gene, for regular qPCR analysis. Their sequences are also included in Table S7 (mNAPRT-F and mNAPRT-R).
To present our figures and results more clearly to the reader, we have made the following modifications in this revision:
(1) We labeled the positions of the aforementioned four primers in Figure S3A (new Supplementary Figure 3a) in green.
(2) We conducted additional qPCR analysis in primary cells and tissues from WT and NAPRT KO mice using both primer sets to show that while the genotyping (GT) primer set failed to amplify the mutant Naprt mRNA in cells/tissues from NAPRT KO mice, the regular primer set revealed comparable levels of Naprt mRNA between WT and KO mice (new Supplementary Figure 3b).
(3) We performed immunoblotting analysis of NAPRT in the liver and colon per the reviewer’s request (new Supplementary Figure 3c). Our results showed that in both liver and colon, the deletion of the 7 amino acids in NAPRT KO mice resulted in a slight down shift of NAPRT protein bands. Moreover, this deletion was coupled with significant protein degradation, particularly in the liver.
We are glad to know that we have addressed all concerns of the reviewer.
For the minor point of the reviewer, we modified the Discussion section to include the following language:

These findings could offer valuable guidance for the development of future NAD-based strategies in cancer prevention and treatment.”
